title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
Otter.ai's transcription service allegedly recorded virtual meetings across multiple platforms by default and sent recordings to the company to improve its AI systems, without alerting meeting participants. The lawsuit claims this occurred despite legal requirements for consent, with users allegedly deceived about what the system does even where privacy policies mention a training checkbox. Whether Otter obtained genuine informed consent and whether its de-identification process adequately protects sensitive information are not established.

The failure is deployment without adequate user awareness and control. A system that collects audio from multiple participants needed explicit opt-in from all of them before recording began, not a buried checkbox or default setting. Automatic enrollment through calendar links made it possible for participants to be recorded without knowing the system was present. Clear notification at meeting start and explicit per-meeting consent would have prevented unknowing participation.

The de-identification of recordings used for AI training is not established to be inadequate. Whether the company's financial benefit from this data collection creates independent legal violations under wiretap and privacy law is a matter for the courts.

Class-action suit claims Otter AI secretly records private work conversations
Otter.ai faces class action lawsuit for unauthorized meeting recording
Enterprise note-taking apps face legal scrutiny as Otter hit with privacy suit

summary:
A federal lawsuit filed on Friday accuses Otter.ai, a Mountain View-based artificial intelligence company, of secretly recording private work conversations without permission. The suit, brought by Justin Brewer of San Jacinto, California, claims the company's transcription service records virtual meetings on Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams by default without alerting participants that their conversations will be shared with Otter to improve its AI systems. The lawsuit alleges this violates state and federal privacy and wiretap laws and contends Otter uses these recordings for financial gain.

Otter.ai serves approximately 25 million users and has processed over 1 billion meetings since its founding in 2016. While the company's privacy policy claims it receives explicit permission through a checkbox for AI training, the lawsuit maintains many users are still deceived. The suit raises concerns about Otter's de-identification process, arguing the company provides no public explanation of how it removes confidential information. Recent complaints have emerged on social media platforms about Otter joining meetings automatically through linked workplace calendars and recording without consent from all participants.
